report.summary: This alert is a true positive. Workstation win81 (192.168.10.5, Windows 8.1, victim LAN) is sending botnet command-and-control traffic over HTTP on port 8080 to 205.174.165.73, an external machine listed as a known attacker. Within ±30 minutes the same two hosts exchanged 130 connections, all to port 8080. Most are small and look alike (about 196 bytes out and 128 bytes back). Several other internal hosts (.8, .9, .14, .15) connect to the same address and port in the same way, so they also look like bots. The detector rates the neighbouring flows as botnet as well. The workstation sent about 963 KB over this channel, far more than check-in traffic alone would explain. That suggests data was uploaded, so the channel was working.

findings.statement: 205.174.165.73 is a public address in the attacker_external zone and is listed as a known attacker ("Kali Linux attacker machine (external)").
192.168.10.5 is win81, a Windows 8.1 64-bit workstation in the victim_lan zone with medium criticality and no listed services.

Within ±30 minutes, 192.168.10.5 sent 130 flows to 205.174.165.73, all on port 8080, between 13:29 and 14:20. In total it sent 963,307 bytes and received 13,931. The alert flow itself was 5 packets and 196 bytes out, 4 packets and 128 bytes back, lasting about 71 ms.

205.174.165.73 received 825 flows within the window, all on port 8080. A search for flows to 205.174.165.73:8080 matched 328 flows; the 60 returned run from 13:40:06 to 13:43:58. They came from several internal hosts (192.168.10.5, .8, .9, .14, .15), mostly 5 packets/about 195 bytes out and 4 packets/128 bytes back, repeating every few tens of seconds. One flow from 192.168.10.8 sent 73,339 bytes.

The detector scored the alert flow at attack probability 0.9999, family botnet. All 10 neighbouring flows it scored between the same two hosts were above the threshold and also classed as botnet (probabilities about 0.998 to 0.9999).

Many internal hosts making repeated, nearly identical small connections to one known attacker address on 8080 looks like bots checking in with a command-and-control server. The workstation's high outbound byte total (963 KB) suggests the channel also carried uploaded data, not just check-ins.

recommended_actions.action: Isolate win81 (192.168.10.5) and look for botnet malware on it (persistence, processes making the port 8080 connections).
Block 205.174.165.73 (at least TCP 8080) at the perimeter firewall.

Extend the investigation to 192.168.10.8, .9, .14 and .15, which show the same beacon pattern to the same address. Check what the large uploads (e.g. 73 KB from .8) contained to see whether data was exfiltrated.

uncertainties: The connection timing was only checked by eye in the first 60 of 328 matched flows, which cover 13:40:06 to 13:43:58. No precise interval analysis was done.
Payloads are not visible, so what the HTTP traffic contained (commands, uploaded data) is not confirmed.
The full list of internal hosts talking to 205.174.165.73 was cut off in the search results, so more infected hosts may exist.
the model asserted the attack succeeded, but no related-events aggregate shows a large return transfer to the source; severity was not raised for it

report.summary: This alert is a true positive: the workstation is beaconing to botnet command-and-control (C2). Workstation win-vista (192.168.10.8) on the internal victim network connects over and over to 205.174.165.73 on port 8080, and that address is listed as a known external attacker (Kali Linux). In the hour around the alert (±30 min), there were 167 flows between the two hosts. The flows are small and look alike, and in the sample returned they repeat roughly every 10 seconds, which is typical of C2 beaconing. Four other internal hosts (192.168.10.5, .9, .14 and .15) send the same flows to the same port, so several machines appear to be infected. The detector rated all 20 neighbouring flows it was asked to re-score as botnet, each with probability around 0.9998.

findings.statement: 205.174.165.73 is a public address in the attacker_external zone and is flagged as a known attacker (Kali Linux attacker machine).
192.168.10.8 is win-vista, a Windows Vista 64-bit workstation in the victim_lan zone with medium criticality and no listed services.

Within ±30 min of the alert, 192.168.10.8 sent 167 flows to 205.174.165.73:8080, totalling 510,099 bytes sent and 14,930 bytes received. The alerted flow itself sent 5 packets (198 bytes), received 4 packets (128 bytes), contained 2 SYN and 2 FIN flags, and lasted about 82 ms.

205.174.165.73:8080 received 799 flows in the same window. An event search returned 121 matching flows, the first at 13:50:01 and the last at 14:03:14, of which 100 were shown. The visible flows are near-identical (about 195 bytes sent, 128 bytes received, 5/4 packets) and come from 192.168.10.5, .8, .9, .14 and .15, with each host repeating about 10 seconds apart.

The detector scored the alert at attack probability 0.99987 (threshold 0.00024) and classed it as botnet. All 20 neighbouring flows between the same two hosts that were re-scored also came out above the threshold as botnet, at about 0.9998 each.

Small, regular, identical connections from several internal workstations to a known attacker host on a non-standard HTTP port point to HTTP C2 beaconing by botnet malware running on multiple compromised hosts. On average each flow sent far more data than the alerted flow (510,099 bytes over 167 flows), which suggests some flows carried larger uploads to the C2 server.

recommended_actions.action: Isolate 192.168.10.8 (win-vista) and do endpoint forensics to find the bot malware and how it persists.
Block 205.174.165.73 (at minimum TCP 8080) at the perimeter firewall.
Treat 192.168.10.5, 192.168.10.9, 192.168.10.14 and 192.168.10.15 as likely infected as well, and isolate and investigate them.
Review the larger outbound flows from 192.168.10.8 to 205.174.165.73 to check whether data was taken out.

uncertainties: There is no payload data, so whether the traffic is really HTTP C2 and which commands were sent is inferred, not observed.
The event search was cut off at 100 of 121 flows, so the roughly 10-second timing comes only from the visible part. Only 20 of the 167 flows between the two hosts were re-scored.
Success is based on repeated completed TCP sessions with replies from the C2 server and a large total of outbound bytes. No individual large flow was inspected to confirm data theft.
the model asserted the attack succeeded, but no related-events aggregate shows a large return transfer to the source; severity was not raised for it

critic: The claim that each host repeats about 10 seconds apart is only partially visible in the truncated sample (e.g., .14 at 13:50:01 then 13:50:11; .9 at :02 then :12), so it is largely supported. However the statement that flows come from exactly hosts .5, .8, .9, .14 and .15 relies on truncated data, and the 'near-identical' pattern is only shown for the visible portion; the 799-flow count in this finding is taken from E3 (same_destination), which is supported.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive. Workstation 192.168.10.14 (win10-pro-32, Windows 10 Pro, victim LAN) is sending repeated small HTTP-style connections on port 8080 to 205.174.165.73. Enrichment lists that address as a known external attacker machine (Kali Linux). There were 160 flows between the two hosts within ±30 minutes, all with nearly identical packet and byte counts, and the server answered every one. Other internal hosts (192.168.10.5, .8, .9 and .15) send the same pattern to the same address on port 8080, so several machines look infected by the same bot. The detector scored all 12 related flows it was given as botnet.

findings.statement: 205.174.165.73 is a public address in the attacker_external zone and is flagged as a known attacker (Kali Linux attacker machine, external).
192.168.10.14 is a private victim_lan host: win10-pro-32, Windows 10 Pro 32-bit, Workstation role, medium criticality.

Within ±30 minutes of the alert there were 160 flows between 192.168.10.14 and 205.174.165.73:8080, from 13:24:28 to 14:20:14. Together they carried 924,152 bytes from the workstation and 17,793 bytes back. The alerted flow had 5 forward packets (195 bytes), 4 backward packets (128 bytes), took about 101 ms and closed normally with FIN.

205.174.165.73:8080 received 825 flows in the ±30 minute window. A flow search to that address and port matched 218 flows and returned the first 100, timestamped 13:45:00 to 13:48:50. Those 100 come from several internal hosts (192.168.10.5, .8, .9, .14, .15). Most are near-identical small sessions of about 195 bytes out and 128 bytes back, arriving every few seconds per host.

The detector scored the alerted flow at an attack probability of 0.99989 against a threshold of 0.00024, as botnet with near-certainty. The top contributing features were Subflow Bwd Bytes = 14, Bwd Init Win Bytes = 237 and Total Length of Bwd Packet = 128.
All 12 related flows between the same two hosts that were re-scored came out above threshold and were classified as botnet.

Regular, repeated small HTTP sessions on non-standard port 8080 to a known attacker host, from several workstations at once, fit botnet command-and-control check-ins. The server answers each session, and far more data goes out than comes back, which suggests the bot channel is active and may be uploading data.

recommended_actions.action: Isolate 192.168.10.14 (win10-pro-32) and investigate it for bot malware, including persistence and running processes.
Block outbound traffic to 205.174.165.73, especially TCP 8080, at the perimeter firewall.
Extend the investigation to 192.168.10.5, 192.168.10.8, 192.168.10.9 and 192.168.10.15, which show the same check-in pattern to 205.174.165.73:8080.
Review the outbound data from 192.168.10.14 (about 924 KB in the hour) for possible data theft.

uncertainties: Without payloads I can't confirm what the traffic contains (HTTP C2 commands, or exactly what data was uploaded).
The flow search was cut off: only 100 of 218 matching flows came back, all between 13:45:00 and 13:48:50. So I haven't fully listed every internal host contacting 205.174.165.73.
I didn't measure the exact check-in interval for 192.168.10.14 alone; regularity is inferred from the sample of flows.
The asset record for 205.174.165.73 is empty; it is known only from enrichment notes.
the model asserted the attack succeeded, but no related-events aggregate shows a large return transfer to the source; severity was not raised for it

critic: The claim that the 100 returned flows are timestamped 13:45:00 to 13:48:50 and come from several internal hosts (.5, .8, .9, .14, .15) is supported by E4. The claim that the sessions arrive "every few seconds per host" is a loose paraphrase of the visible timestamps. However, the claim that "Most are near-identical small sessions" is based only on a truncated sample, and E4's data is cut off. This is borderline but acceptable. The more clear problem is the "205.174.165.73:8080 received 825 flows" claim, which E3 supports as same_destination count 825. No clear unsupported claim found in this finding.

report.summary: Workstation win10-64 (192.168.10.15) looks infected with a botnet and is beaconing to a known attacker C2 host. Within ±30 minutes it sent 200 small TCP flows to 205.174.165.73:8080, the external Kali attacker machine. In the flows I could see, they arrive about every 10 seconds and are nearly the same size. Hosts 192.168.10.9 and 192.168.10.14 show the same timing at the start of the window. Every neighbouring flow from this host that I re-scored came back as botnet. The flows carry nothing else, so I can't confirm that commands ran or that data was taken.

findings.statement: 205.174.165.73 is a public address in the attacker_external zone and is flagged as a known attacker (Kali Linux attacker machine).
192.168.10.15 is win10-64, a Windows 10 64-bit workstation in victim_lan with medium criticality and no listed services.

Within ±30 minutes of the alert, 192.168.10.15 sent 200 flows to 205.174.165.73, all on port 8080, from 13:32:03 to 14:31:53. Together they total 1,122,699 bytes sent and 16,608 bytes received. The alerted flow itself was 5 packets/195 bytes out, 4 packets/128 bytes back, and lasted 131 ms.

In the search results I received (13:32:00–13:40:29), this host's flows are spaced about 10 seconds apart (13:32:03, 13:32:13, …). They return 4–5 packets of 128–131 bytes and usually send about 195 bytes, though some send about 1 KB.

205.174.165.73:8080 received 766 flows within ±30 minutes of the alert (13:32:00–14:31:54), all on port 8080. The source breakdown is not given. My one-hour search matched 767 flows but returned only the first 200 (13:32:00–13:40:29). In those, 192.168.10.9 (13:32:00, 13:32:10, 13:32:20) and 192.168.10.14 (13:32:02, 13:32:12, 13:32:22) also connect about every 10 seconds, with similar small reply sizes.

The detector scored the alerted flow as botnet with attack probability 0.9998. I re-scored 15 neighbouring flows between the same two hosts: all 15 crossed the alert threshold and all were predicted botnet.
Regular, small, same-size flows from at least three internal hosts to one known attacker on non-standard port 8080 match botnet C2 beaconing.
In the same window, 192.168.10.15 also sent 2,911 flows to 364 IPs on 17 ports, mostly 53, 80 and 443, plus a few on 22, 445, 135, 137 and 389.

recommended_actions.action: Isolate win10-64 (192.168.10.15) and collect forensic evidence from it, including the program that opens connections to port 8080.
Block 205.174.165.73 at the perimeter firewall.
Triage 192.168.10.9 and 192.168.10.14 as possible bots, since they beacon to the same C2 host.
Review this host's traffic on ports 445, 135, 137, 389 and 22 for signs of lateral movement.

uncertainties: The flow records carry no payloads, so I can't confirm that commands ran or that data left the network.
I only received the first 200 of 767 destination flows (13:32–13:40). I can't confirm the full list of internal sources or their timing for the rest of the hour.
I didn't check whether this host's wider activity is unusual for a workstation.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive: an FTP brute-force attempt against web-server-16 (192.168.10.50). Around the alert time, 172.16.0.1 sent 2,479 flows to this one server, and 2,478 of them went to port 21 (FTP). That source address is the firewall's inside address. Attacker traffic from outside is translated (NAT) to this address, and the address is flagged as a known attacker. The target is a high-criticality public web server running FTP. All 9 neighbouring flows the detector scored also alerted as brute_force. Nothing shows that a login worked.

findings.statement: Within ±30 minutes, 172.16.0.1 sent 2,479 flows to just one host, 192.168.10.50. 2,478 went to port 21 and 1 to port 80. Activity ran from 12:42:19 to 13:30:03. The flows were small: 297,402 bytes sent in total and 465,584 bytes received, which works out to about 120 bytes out and 188 bytes back per session.
The alerted flow (event 1167428) lasted about 9.7 s. It had 11 packets / 122 bytes outbound and 17 packets / 188 bytes back, with 2 SYN, 2 FIN and 2 RST flags.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside (NAT) address and is flagged as a known attacker. Attacker traffic from outside appears in the flow records under this source address.

192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04 in the victim LAN, with high criticality. Its services are HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22. Inventory notes list it as the target of FTP/SSH brute force.

Across all sources, 192.168.10.50 received 2,733 flows, seen between 12:42:19 and 13:41:45. These included 146 flows to port 22 and 44 to port 139. The flows from 172.16.0.1 itself went only to ports 21 and 80. The results do not say which addresses sent the port 22 and 139 flows.

The detector gave the alerted flow an attack probability of 0.99994 and classed it as brute_force (0.999998). All 9 neighbouring flows that were scored also alerted as brute_force, each with probability of about 0.9999.
Thousands of short, near-identical FTP sessions that end in resets and return about 11 bytes per packet look like automated password guessing that keeps failing. Nothing points to a successful login.

recommended_actions.action: Check the FTP authentication logs on web-server-16 for any successful login between 12:42 and 13:31 on 2017-07-04, and reset any accounts that may be affected.
At the perimeter, block or rate-limit the external sources behind the NAT address 172.16.0.1. Use firewall NAT logs to find the original attacker IPs.
Restrict or turn off FTP exposure on this high-criticality server, and enforce account lockout or fail2ban on FTP and SSH.

uncertainties: The flow records have no payloads or authentication results, so I can't confirm whether any login worked.
Because of NAT, the original external attacker IPs are hidden behind 172.16.0.1.
I didn't look up CVEs because the FTP server software and version are not in the inventory.
Only 9 of the 2,479 neighbouring flows were scored by the detector.
The results don't show who sent the port 22 and 139 flows to the server, so I can't tell whether they belong to the same campaign.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive: an FTP password-guessing attack (brute force) against web-server-16 (192.168.10.50), a high-criticality host. Within ±30 minutes, 172.16.0.1 sent 2,398 flows to this one host, and 2,397 of them went to FTP port 21. Each session is short and carries little data. 172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address, and traffic from external attackers appears under it after NAT. All 10 neighbouring flows I scored were also flagged as brute_force. The data sizes stay uniform across the burst, so nothing shows a login succeeded.

findings.statement: Within ±30 minutes of event 1201829, 172.16.0.1 sent 2,398 flows, all to 192.168.10.50. 2,397 went to port 21 and 1 to port 80, between 12:43:38 and 13:30:03. Total bytes were 287,860 sent and 450,356 received.
The alerted flow lasted about 8,560 ms. It sent 11 packets (123 bytes) and got 17 packets (188 bytes) back, with 2 SYN, 2 FIN and 2 RST flags.
A short TCP session with little data, followed by RST, fits one automated login attempt. Received bytes average about 188 per flow (450,356 / 2,398), which suggests the sessions are uniform.
In the same window, 192.168.10.50 received 2,654 flows across 35 destination ports, including 150 to port 22 and 44 to port 139. Flows from 172.16.0.1 went only to ports 21 and 80.
From the counts, the port 22 and port 139 flows to the destination did not come from 172.16.0.1. Their sources were not identified.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address and is flagged as a known attacker: traffic from external attackers appears under this address after NAT.

192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04 with HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22. Its criticality is high, it sits in the victim LAN, and its inventory notes name it as the target of FTP/SSH brute force.

The detector gave the alerted flow an attack probability of 0.99994 and a brute_force family probability of 0.999998. All 10 neighbouring same-pair flows I scored were above threshold and predicted brute_force.
Thousands of near-identical short sessions to FTP port 21 from one source to one host is the pattern of automated password guessing (ATT&CK T1110.001). Nothing shows a login succeeding.

recommended_actions.action: Find the external source addresses behind the NAT using the firewall's NAT and connection logs, then block them at the perimeter.
Check the FTP authentication logs on web-server-16 for any successful login during 12:43–13:30 on 2017-07-04. If any account logged in, reset its credentials.
Turn on failed-login rate limiting or lockout (for example fail2ban) for FTP and SSH on web-server-16. Consider turning off plain FTP or limiting who can reach it.

uncertainties: Flow records hold no FTP application data, so they don't show whether any login worked. Only the uniform data sizes suggest the attempts failed.
Only 10 of the 2,397 FTP flows were scored with the detector.
I didn't look up CVEs because the inventory doesn't say which FTP server software is running.
The original external attacker IP is hidden behind the firewall's NAT.
The sources of the port 22 and port 139 flows to the destination were not identified.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive: an FTP brute-force attack against web-server-16 (192.168.10.50), a high-criticality server. In the 30 minutes either side of the alert, 172.16.0.1 opened 2,381 connections to this server, 2,380 of them on port 21. That source address is the firewall's inside address, and the enrichment notes say outside attackers appear under it because of address translation (NAT). The detector rated the alerted flow and all 10 sampled neighbouring flows as brute_force with a probability of about 0.99993. Nothing shows a login succeeded. The flows are all about the same size (roughly 188 bytes back from the server each), which fits repeated failed login attempts.

findings.statement: From 12:43:53 to 13:30:03, 172.16.0.1 sent 2,381 flows to one destination, 192.168.10.50: 2,380 to port 21 and 1 to port 80. Together they carried 285,830 bytes forward and 447,160 bytes back.
The alerted flow (event 1212114) lasted 8.6 s with 11 packets and 120 bytes forward, 17 packets and 188 bytes back, and 2 each of SYN, FIN and RST flags.
In the same window, 192.168.10.50 also received traffic on ports 22 (150 flows), 139 (44 flows) and about 35 distinct ports overall. Some of this came from sources other than 172.16.0.1.

192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04. Its criticality is high and it sits in the victim LAN zone. It runs HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22, and the inventory notes list it as a target of FTP/SSH brute force.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address and is flagged as a known attacker. Outside attackers show up under this address because of NAT.

The detector scored the alerted flow at an attack probability of 0.99994 against a threshold of 0.00024, with a brute_force family probability of 0.999998. The strongest contributing features were Bwd Packet Length Mean, Bwd RST Flags and Fwd IAT Min.
All 10 sampled neighbouring flows on the same pair scored above the threshold and were classified as brute_force (probability about 0.99993 to 0.99994).

Thousands of short, near-identical FTP connections from one source to one target over about 47 minutes match automated password guessing against FTP. On average each flow carried about 188 bytes back from the server, the same as the alerted flow. That points to repeated rejected logins rather than a successful session.

recommended_actions.action: Pull the FTP server's authentication logs on web-server-16 for 12:43–13:31 on 2017-07-04. Check for any successful login, and for any session that is much longer or larger than the rest.
Use the firewall's NAT logs to find the real outside source behind 172.16.0.1, then block it at the perimeter. Do not block 172.16.0.1 itself, because that would cut off all translated traffic.
Limit login attempts or lock accounts after repeated FTP failures, and consider whether FTP needs to be reachable from outside on this high-criticality server.
Check the SSH (22) and SMB (139) traffic to 192.168.10.50 in the same window for related credential attacks.

uncertainties: There is no payload or FTP log data, so I can't confirm the login attempts or rule out a successful login. The conclusion that no login succeeded rests only on the uniform flow sizes.
Because of NAT, the real outside source address isn't visible.
I didn't look up CVEs: the inventory doesn't name the FTP server software or its version, so a relevant CVE couldn't be identified.
The detector scored only 10 of the 2,381 neighbouring flows.
The flow records don't say which source sent the port 22, 139 and other traffic to the server.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive: an SSH brute-force attack against web-server-16 (192.168.10.50), a high-criticality Ubuntu 16.04 server. Between 17:34:28 and 18:11:20 on 2017-07-04, the source 172.16.0.1 opened 1,768 flows to port 22 on this one host and nothing else. That address is the firewall's inside address, and attacker traffic coming in from outside shows up under it. The flows I sampled all look alike: about 22-24 forward packets, 2,008 forward bytes and multi-second durations. That is what repeated scripted login attempts look like. The detector scores the alerted flow and all 10 sampled neighbouring flows as brute_force with a probability close to 1. There is no flow-level sign that a login succeeded.

findings.statement: Within ±30 minutes of event 1225179, 172.16.0.1 sent 1,768 flows to 192.168.10.50, all to port 22, between 17:34:28 and 18:11:20. It contacted no other destination IP or port.
The anchor flow lasted about 11.7 s, with 23 forward and 33 backward packets, 2,008 forward bytes and 2,745 backward bytes, and it closed normally with FIN.
In the same window, 192.168.10.50 also received traffic on port 21 (88 flows), port 139 (54 flows) and dozens of other ports, out of 2,154 flows to that destination in total.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside (NAT) address and is flagged as a known attacker: external attacker traffic appears with this source address.

192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04 in the victim LAN, with high criticality. Its known services are HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22, and the inventory notes list it as a target of the FTP/SSH brute force.

The detector gives the alerted flow an attack probability of 0.99994 against a threshold of 0.00024, with family brute_force at 0.999998. The strongest contributing features are Fwd PSH Flags=16 and Bwd Init Win Bytes=247.
All 10 sampled neighbouring flows on the same pair and port 22 score above threshold and are classified as brute_force. Each has nearly the same features (2,008 forward bytes, 22-24 forward packets).
About 1,768 nearly identical SSH sessions from one source to one host in about 37 minutes points to automated password guessing, not legitimate administration.

recommended_actions.action: Block or rate-limit SSH from external sources to 192.168.10.50 at the firewall. Because the traffic is NATed, trace the real external source addresses in the firewall/NAT logs.

Check SSH auth logs (/var/log/auth.log) on web-server-16 for successful logins between 17:34 and 18:12 UTC on 2017-07-04. Reset credentials for any accounts that were targeted, and require key-based authentication plus fail2ban or a similar tool.
Investigate the FTP/21 and other-port traffic to the same host in the same window, since it may be related brute-force or scanning activity.

uncertainties: Flow data cannot show whether any SSH login succeeded. The sampled flows look the same size, which points to failed attempts, but host auth logs are needed to confirm.
The real external source addresses are hidden behind the firewall NAT address 172.16.0.1.
Only 10 of the 1,768 related flows were scored with predict_attack, and part of that output was truncated.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive: an HTTP flood (DDoS) against web-server-16 (192.168.10.50), a high-criticality public web server. Its traffic arrives through the firewall's NAT address, 172.16.0.1. Within ±30 minutes of the alert, 172.16.0.1 opened 95,143 flows to 192.168.10.50:80 between 18:56:31 and 19:16:10, about 80 per second. Each flow sent almost nothing (20 forward bytes in the alert's own flow), while the server sent back about 1.1 GB in total. Enrichment lists 172.16.0.1 as the firewall inside address, which stands in for the external attackers. The detector rated the alert, and all 20 neighbouring flows it scored, as DDoS with probability above 0.9999.

findings.statement: Within ±30 minutes, 172.16.0.1 sent 95,143 flows to 192.168.10.50 on port 80 between 18:56:31Z and 19:16:10Z, about 80 flows per second. Those flows carried 1,902,900 forward bytes and 1,109,610,790 backward bytes. The alert's own flow sent 8 packets and 20 bytes and got back 6 packets and 11,595 bytes in 3.88 seconds.

192.168.10.50 received 95,415 flows in total in the window, and 95,143 of them came from 172.16.0.1. Other sources made up only about 272 flows (mostly to ports 22, 21 and 139), so nearly all the HTTP volume comes through the NAT address.
192.168.10.50 is web-server-16: a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04 in the victim_lan zone, with high criticality and services HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address and is flagged as a known attacker. Traffic from external attackers shows up under this address because of NAT.

The detector scored the alert flow at attack probability 0.99991, far above the 0.00024 threshold, with family ddos at 0.99999. The strongest features were Bwd Packet Length Std, Packet Length Std and Fwd Packet Length Max of 20.
All 20 neighbouring flows on the same pair that were scored came out above the threshold and were classed as ddos, each with attack probability of about 0.99996.

Many tiny, repeated HTTP requests that each pull a large response, at about 80 flows per second for roughly 20 minutes, look like a flood meant to exhaust a web server. Because of NAT, the flood can be distributed even though it shows a single source address.

recommended_actions.action: At the perimeter, rate-limit or filter inbound HTTP to web-server-16 (public IP 205.174.165.68), using DDoS mitigation or upstream scrubbing if available.
Pull the firewall/NAT translation logs for 18:56–19:17Z on 2017-07-07 to find the real external source addresses behind 172.16.0.1, then block them.
Check web-server-16's availability, web server logs and resource use for the attack window to see whether service was actually degraded.
Review the small amount of other inbound traffic to 192.168.10.50 on SSH, FTP and SMB in the same window for related activity.

uncertainties: NAT hides the real external sources, so the number of attacking hosts (DDoS versus single-source DoS) cannot be seen in the flow data.
There is no availability or service-health evidence for the server, so it is unknown whether the flood actually degraded service. Large response volume only shows the server kept answering.
Only 20 sampled neighbouring flows were scored; the rest of the roughly 95k flows were not individually scored.

critic: The claim of 'about 80 flows per second' is not in the evidence summary or data. The 'within ±30 minutes' framing is also loose, since the pair first_seen and last_seen span 18:56:31Z to 19:16:10Z. report.summary: Event 2173685 is part of a large application-layer DoS flood against the web server web-server-16 (192.168.10.50). The source address, 172.16.0.1, is the firewall's inside address. External attacker traffic shows up under this address after NAT. Within ±30 minutes, 168,028 flows went from this address to the server, all but one to port 80. No other destination was contacted. Every neighbouring flow I scored was flagged as DoS. The flood is aimed at one high-value server, and I found no sign of a wider campaign from this source.

findings.statement: Within ±30 minutes of the event, 172.16.0.1 sent 168,028 flows to 192.168.10.50, between 13:28:26 and 14:19:49 (about 51 minutes, roughly 55 flows per second). 168,027 went to port 80 and 1 to port 0. Totals were about 70.4 MB forward and 1.91 GB backward. The source contacted only this one destination.

The alerted flow itself was short and small: 54 ms, 8 forward packets (339 bytes), 7 backward packets (11,595 bytes), with 2 SYN, 2 FIN and 3 RST flags. This is a quick connect-request-teardown pattern repeated at very high volume.

172.16.0.1 is a private address in the firewall zone and is marked as a known attacker. The enrichment notes say it is the firewall's inside address: external attacker traffic appears under it after NAT, so it is not the firewall acting on its own.

192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04 with HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22. Its criticality is high and it sits in the victim LAN zone. The inventory notes list it as a target of DoS, DDoS, brute-force and web attacks.

The detector scored the alerted flow at an attack probability of 0.99996, against a threshold of 0.00024, and labelled it DoS (0.99999). The biggest drivers were Bwd Packet Length Std and Packet Length Std.

I scored 10 neighbouring flows on the same source-destination pair. All 10 were above the threshold and labelled DoS, with attack probabilities between about 0.83 and 0.999. Several had no backward payload and 3 SYN flags, which fits half-open or slow connections.

Six figures together point to an HTTP DoS flood rather than normal browsing: the steady ~55 flows per second, one source, one destination, one port, short repeated connections, and some flows with no backward payload. This matches DoS tools of the Hulk, GoldenEye or Slowloris/Slowhttptest type. The large backward byte total shows the server was still answering many requests, but it does not show whether the service was degraded.

The same-destination totals include a few flows to ports 22, 21 and 139 and to high ports. None of these came from 172.16.0.1, which only used port 80 and port 0. So the evidence points to one targeted flood from this source, not a multi-target campaign.

recommended_actions.action: At the perimeter firewall, rate-limit or block the external source addresses that are NAT'd to 172.16.0.1 for HTTP traffic to web-server-16. Use the firewall's pre-NAT logs to find the real external addresses.
Check web-server-16's availability and resource logs (Apache/web server error logs, connection-table exhaustion) from 13:28 to 14:20 on 2017-07-05 to find out whether service was degraded.
Harden the HTTP service against slow and flood DoS: per-IP connection limits, shorter request timeouts (for example mod_reqtimeout), or a reverse proxy or WAF in front of the server.

uncertainties: The real external source address(es) are hidden behind the firewall NAT (172.16.0.1). The flow records cannot tell one attacker from several.
There is no direct evidence that the service became unavailable (no availability or server-side logs), so success_indicator is false.
I did not look up CVEs. The web server software and version on 192.168.10.50 are not in the inventory, so no CVE can be linked to it.
Flow features alone cannot say which DoS tool was used (Hulk, GoldenEye, Slowloris or Slowhttptest).

report.summary: This alert is a real attack: a single-source HTTP denial-of-service (DoS) flood against web-server-16 (192.168.10.50:80). report.summary: This alert is a real internal port scan. The workstation 192.168.10.8 (win-vista) sent 596 flows to another workstation, 192.168.10.19 (ubuntu-14-32), covering 397 distinct destination ports in about 28 minutes. The alerted flow is a scan probe. It went to port 8333, carried no payload in either direction, and the target answered with two RST packets, which means the port was closed. Over the same hour the source also reached 495 IPs and 1,054 ports. Neither host is a known attacker. A normal workstation scanning the LAN like this suggests 192.168.10.8 may be compromised or misused. There is no sign that the scan led to a successful exploit.

findings.statement: The alerted flow 3105744 (192.168.10.8:59793 -> 192.168.10.19:8333/TCP) lasted 0.075 ms. It had 2 forward and 2 backward packets, 0 bytes in each direction, 2 SYN flags and 2 RST flags.

Within ±30 minutes, 192.168.10.8 sent 596 flows to 192.168.10.19 on 397 distinct destination ports, between 18:12:32 and 18:40:59. Ports included 139, 445, 1, 12657, 24696 and 137. Overall the source sent 9,995 flows to 495 IPs on 1,054 distinct ports.

192.168.10.8 is win-vista, a Windows Vista workstation in victim_lan with medium criticality. 192.168.10.19 is ubuntu-14-32, an Ubuntu 14.04 workstation in victim_lan with medium criticality and no listed services. Neither is a known attacker.
The target replied to the port 8333 probe with RST and no payload, so the port was closed. This was a probe, not Bitcoin traffic. The inventory also lists no services on 192.168.10.19.
The detector scored the alerted flow at 0.99994 attack probability, classed as port_scan (0.999998). The strongest factors were zero backward packet length, Bwd RST Flags=2 and Fwd IAT Min=48.
All 10 sampled neighbouring flows between the same two hosts scored above the threshold and were classed as port_scan, each at roughly 0.9999 probability.
A workstation sweeping hundreds of ports and hosts inside the LAN is not normal behaviour. It suggests 192.168.10.8 may be compromised and being used for internal discovery.

recommended_actions.action: Isolate or closely monitor 192.168.10.8 (win-vista) and examine it for compromise: running processes, scanning tools and how it was first infected.
Check whether 192.168.10.8 made follow-up connections that got real responses, especially on SMB ports 139 and 445, to 192.168.10.19 or the other 494 hosts it scanned.
Block or alert on peer-to-peer scanning between workstations in victim_lan.

uncertainties: Only 10 of the 596 flows between the two hosts were scored by the detector.
Some of the source's 9,995 flows are probably ordinary traffic (DNS, HTTPS), so not all of its activity is scanning.
I did not check whether any scanned port returned a non-trivial response, so I cannot tell if the scan led to further exploitation.
Flow data cannot show what initially compromised 192.168.10.8.

report.summary: This alert is a real internal port scan. 192.168.10.8 (win-vista, a Windows Vista workstation on the victim LAN) sent short, empty SYN flows to many ports on 192.168.10.5 (win81, a Windows 8.1 workstation). Within ±30 minutes it also produced 9,580 flows to 495 IPs across 1,045 ports. The alerted flow lasted 0.046 ms and contained 2 SYN packets with no payload and no reply. The neighbouring flows on the same host pair, which hit ports 9999, 8254, 2323 and 1151 within a few seconds, follow the same pattern. All 10 of them also score as port_scan. win81 lists no services, so there is no sign that anything on port 6669 (an IRC port) answered. The pattern matches T1046 Network Service Discovery. Because the scan comes from an inventoried workstation that is not a known attacker or a scanning host, that workstation may be compromised and is now scanning the LAN from inside.

findings.statement: The anchor flow 3105831 (192.168.10.8:65231 to 192.168.10.5:6669/TCP) is recorded as: duration_ms 0.046, fwd_packets 2, syn_count 2, fwd_bytes 0, bwd_packets 0, bwd_bytes 0, rst_count 0.

Within ±30 minutes, 192.168.10.8 generated 9,580 flows to 495 distinct IPs and 1,045 distinct ports, between 18:12 and 19:12 UTC. Toward 192.168.10.5 alone it sent 107 flows to 30 distinct ports, totalling 11,600 bytes forward and only 192 bytes back.

Between 18:42:35 and 18:42:46, 26 flows went from 192.168.10.8 to 192.168.10.5. They included single-SYN, zero-byte probes to ports 6669, 9999, 8254, 2323 and 1151, plus repeated SYN/RST exchanges on port 135.
192.168.10.8 is win-vista, a Windows Vista 64-bit workstation on the victim LAN with medium criticality. It is not flagged as a known attacker.
192.168.10.5 is win81, a Windows 8.1 64-bit workstation on the victim LAN with medium criticality and no listed services.

The detector gave the anchor flow an attack probability of 0.999, far above the 0.00024 threshold, with port_scan probability ≈0.99999. All 10 neighbouring flows on the same host pair also scored above threshold as port_scan.
An inventoried workstation sweeping hundreds of hosts and ports is consistent with T1046 Network Service Discovery from a likely compromised internal host. Nothing suggests an authorised scanner.

recommended_actions.action: Isolate 192.168.10.8 (win-vista) and examine it for compromise, such as malware or a remote-access tool. A workstation should not be generating LAN-wide scans.

Check the hosts and ports that answered the scan (for example the replies on port 135 from 192.168.10.5) for any follow-on connections from 192.168.10.8 after 18:42 UTC that could indicate lateral movement.
Block or alert on further scanning from 192.168.10.8 at internal segmentation points while the investigation is open.

uncertainties: I don't know how 192.168.10.8 was originally compromised; these flows only show the discovery stage.
I didn't check the other 494 targeted hosts one by one, or look for exploitation after the scan.
Some of the predict_attack and search_events output was truncated, so not every neighbouring flow could be reviewed.

critic: The finding describes the probes to ports 6669, 9999, 8254, 2323 and 1151 as "single-SYN". The cited data shows syn_count 2 and fwd_packets 2 for each of those flows, so "single-SYN" is not supported and contradicts the data.

report.summary: Internal workstation 192.168.10.8 (win-vista) ran a TCP port scan against workstation 192.168.10.9 (win7-pro). The alerted flow is to port 445. It carried no payload: it had 8 SYNs, the target sent back 2 RSTs, and 0 bytes moved in either direction. Within ±30 minutes the same pair had 1,229 flows across 623 destination ports. Over the same window the source reached 520 hosts on 1,028 ports. All 10 neighbouring flows I re-scored also alerted as port_scan. This is internal discovery (lateral reconnaissance) coming from a victim-LAN host, so the source host may be compromised. I found no sign that SMB was exploited or that the scan got anything beyond probe responses.

findings.statement: The anchor flow 3120557 went from 192.168.10.8:60467 to 192.168.10.9:445/TCP. It lasted about 21 seconds, with 8 SYN flags, 2 RST flags, 2 forward and 8 backward packets, and 0 bytes in each direction.

Within ±30 minutes, 192.168.10.8 sent 1,229 flows to 192.168.10.9 across 623 distinct destination ports (top ports: 1026, 1037, 1042, 1041, 135 and 445). In total the pair exchanged only 51,066 forward and 38,888 backward bytes.
In the same window, 192.168.10.8 produced 9,351 flows to 520 distinct IPs on 1,028 distinct ports. That includes 179 flows to 445, 180 to 139 and 216 to 135.

Both hosts are in the victim LAN and neither is a known attacker. 192.168.10.8 is win-vista (Windows Vista workstation, medium criticality) and 192.168.10.9 is win7-pro (Windows 7 Pro workstation, medium criticality). The inventory lists no services for either host.

The detector scored the anchor flow at attack probability 0.9998 against a threshold of 0.00024, with family port_scan at 0.99999. The main contributing features were zero backward packet length, SYN count and backward RST flags.
I re-scored 10 neighbouring flows between the same pair. All 10 were above threshold and classified as port_scan.

A single source probing hundreds of ports on one host, and hundreds of hosts overall, with SYNs answered by RSTs and no payload, is a network service discovery scan, not normal SMB use. The scan comes from an internal workstation, so win-vista is likely compromised and being used for lateral reconnaissance.
The anchor flow moved 0 bytes and got only RSTs back, so it shows no successful SMB session or exploitation.

recommended_actions.action: Isolate 192.168.10.8 (win-vista) and examine it for compromise: running processes, scanning tools, recent logons and persistence. It is scanning 520 internal hosts.
Look for follow-on activity from 192.168.10.8 to the scanned hosts, such as data-bearing sessions on 445, 139 or 135, that would show exploitation after the scan.
Check that 192.168.10.9 and other LAN workstations are patched for SMB and are not exposing 445 when they don't need to.

uncertainties: I did not look up T1021.002 (SMB/Windows Admin Shares) or CVE-2017-0144, so neither is cited. The flows show scanning only, not SMB exploitation.
How 192.168.10.8 was first compromised, and whether it is an authorised scanner, cannot be told from flow data or the asset inventory.
Part of the re-scoring output was cut off in the tool response. The summary still states that all 10 flows were above threshold.
The source's heavy DNS (port 53) and HTTPS (port 443) traffic, about 50 MB received, was not investigated. It may be normal browsing mixed in with the scan.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive: an internal port scan from workstation 192.168.10.8 (win-vista, Windows Vista) against 192.168.10.19 (ubuntu-14-32). Within ±30 minutes, the same source sent 596 flows to 397 distinct ports on this target, and 9995 flows to 495 IPs and 1054 ports overall. The alerted flow to TCP 1524 was a single SYN/RST probe that carried no payload in either direction, so the port was closed. All 10 neighbouring flows to the same target that I scored also alerted as port_scan. A user workstation scanning the LAN this widely is not normal behaviour, so the source host is probably compromised. It is not a known attacker address.

findings.statement: Anchor flow 3174517: 192.168.10.8:59793 -> 192.168.10.19:1524/TCP. It lasted 0.092 ms, with 2 SYN, 2 RST, 0 forward bytes and 0 backward bytes. An event search for flows from this source to 192.168.10.19 on port 1524 matched only this flow.

Within ±30 minutes, 192.168.10.8 generated 9995 flows to 495 destination IPs and 1054 distinct ports. Of these, 596 went to 192.168.10.19 across 397 distinct ports between 18:12:32 and 18:40:59. The busiest ports on this target were 139, 445, 1, 12657 and 24696.
192.168.10.8 is win-vista, a Windows Vista 64-bit workstation in victim_lan with medium criticality. It is not flagged as a known attacker.
192.168.10.19 is ubuntu-14-32, an Ubuntu 14.04 32-bit workstation in victim_lan with medium criticality. The inventory lists no services for it, including nothing on TCP 1524.

The detector scored the alert flow at attack probability 0.99994 (threshold 0.00024), with port_scan family probability about 0.999998. The main drivers were zero backward packet length, backward RST flags and zero forward payload.
All 10 sampled neighbouring flows from 192.168.10.8 to 192.168.10.19 scored above threshold and were classified as port_scan.

A workstation probing hundreds of ports on one host and hundreds of hosts on the LAN matches T1046 Network Service Discovery. The scan most likely comes from a compromised workstation rather than an authorised scanner, since nothing in the asset record says it is one.

The target refused the probe to 1524 with RST and sent no data back, so there is no sign of an open backdoor on that port or of exploitation through it. The pair did exchange about 37.9 KB of backward bytes in total, which most likely came from SMB/NetBIOS replies (ports 139/445), but I did not examine those flows.

recommended_actions.action: Isolate 192.168.10.8 (win-vista) for triage and forensic review: find the scanning process, check for persistence, and work out how it was compromised. It is scanning the LAN widely, and the asset record does not say it is an authorised scanner.
Check the flows from 192.168.10.8 to 192.168.10.19 that got non-RST responses, especially on 139/445, for signs of follow-on access to the Ubuntu host.
Review the other 494 hosts this source contacted, and its heavy DNS (53) and HTTPS (443) traffic, for lateral movement or command-and-control.

uncertainties: I did not run a CVE or backdoor lookup for port 1524. Because the probe was refused with RST, a CVE tied to that port would not change the verdict.
I did not inspect the individual same-pair flows that had backward bytes, so it is unconfirmed whether any port on 192.168.10.19 was open or exploited.
The available data doesn't show whether 192.168.10.8 is an authorised scanner. The asset record shows only a standard workstation.
Only 10 of the 596 same-pair flows were scored by the model.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive. Attacker traffic came in through the firewall/NAT address 172.16.0.1 and hit ubuntu-server-12 (192.168.10.51) on TCP port 444. That host is high-criticality, runs Ubuntu 12.04 and has an OpenSSL service on port 444, and the asset notes list a scheduled Heartbleed attack against that port. The traffic is a series of long-lived connections to port 444 only, each very lopsided: the anchor flow sent 7,920 bytes and got back 7,883,880 bytes. Across the flows aggregated for this source-destination pair, about 33 MB came back. That pattern fits Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160) leaking server memory. The detector flags all the scored flows, but labels the family web_attack, which looks like the wrong family.

findings.statement: 192.168.10.51 is ubuntu-server-12: a server running Ubuntu 12.04, criticality high, in the victim_lan zone, with an OpenSSL service on port 444. Its asset notes say a Heartbleed attack against port 444 on this host is scheduled.

The related-events aggregate for ±10 minutes reports 5 flows each for the same source, the same destination and the same pair. All of them go to 192.168.10.51 on port 444 only, between 18:22:16 and 18:32:18 UTC, with 40,476 bytes forward and 33,127,315 bytes back in total. The sample event ids listed are 2248767, 2249516, 2249898, 2250775 and 2345656. The anchor flow is reported separately: about 119 s long, with 2,796 forward packets totalling 7,920 bytes and 2,007 backward packets totalling 7,883,880 bytes.

All 5 sampled flows for this source-destination pair scored above the alert threshold, with probabilities from 0.0145 to 0.996 and a predicted family of web_attack. The main driver in every case was high Bwd Packet Length Std. The anchor flow scored 0.7126.
CVE-2014-0160 (Heartbleed, CVSS 7.5) is an OpenSSL heartbeat buffer over-read that lets a remote attacker read process memory.

Many small repeated requests that draw megabytes of response from an OpenSSL service fit Heartbleed memory leakage, not a web attack. The detector's web_attack label is probably the closest family it has for this traffic. The size of the responses suggests memory contents were actually leaked.

recommended_actions.action: Patch or upgrade OpenSSL on ubuntu-server-12 to 1.0.1g or later, or take the port 444 service offline until it is patched.
Assume server memory was exposed: revoke and reissue the TLS private keys and certificates for the port 444 service, and rotate any credentials or session secrets it handled.
Block or restrict inbound access to port 444 at the firewall. Use the firewall's NAT logs to identify the real external source behind 172.16.0.1.

uncertainties: The related-events data doesn't say whether the 5-flow count includes the anchor flow, although the anchor's event id is not among the sample ids.
There is no payload inspection, so I can't confirm the requests were malformed heartbeat requests. The Heartbleed conclusion rests on asset context and flow byte asymmetry.
The detector's family label (web_attack) doesn't match the likely Heartbleed activity.
I can't see exactly what memory contents leaked.

critic: The finding says the aggregate shows 5 flows 'each' and that all flows go to port 444 between 18:22:16 and 18:32:18, with the specified bytes and sample ids, which the data supports. However the claim that the window is ±10 minutes while the first_seen/last_seen spans about 10 minutes beyond the anchor (18:30:17) is consistent; the anchor's 7,920 forward bytes and 7,883,880 backward bytes match. No unsupported claim found in this item.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive for botnet command-and-control (C2) traffic. The internal Windows Vista workstation win-vista (192.168.10.8) kept a session open for about 40 minutes, from 18:04 to 18:44, to 205.174.165.73 on port 444. That address is a known attacker, the Kali Linux machine in the external attacker range. Across 16 flows from the same source port, the workstation sent 110,404 bytes and got back only 282, a beacon-like pattern. A second host, 192.168.10.25, also contacted the same address and port, first with SYN/RST attempts every 10 seconds and then with an established session. The detector flagged all 16 flows between the pair, though it named different attack families for different flows.

findings.statement: 205.174.165.73 is a public address in zone attacker_external and is listed as a known attacker (Kali Linux attacker machine, external).
192.168.10.8 is win-vista, a Windows Vista 64-bit workstation in victim_lan with medium criticality and no listed services.

Within ±30 minutes there were 16 flows from 192.168.10.8 to 205.174.165.73:444, all from source port 1260, seen from 18:04:25 to 18:44:24. Together they sent 110,404 bytes forward and received 282 bytes back. The alert flow itself lasted about 118 s, with 45 forward packets (15,738 bytes) and 40 backward packets carrying 0 bytes.

A second internal host, 192.168.10.25, also contacted 205.174.165.73:444. It made SYN/RST connection attempts at exact 10-second intervals from 18:03:05 to 18:04:15, then opened a session at 18:04:25 that received 285 bytes back.
In the same window, 192.168.10.8 also produced a large amount of other traffic: 10,376 flows to 484 IPs on 1,074 ports. The top ports were 53, 443, 80, 135, 139 and 445.

The detector gave the alert flow an attack probability of 0.996 and labelled it botnet with probability 0.995. The strongest contributing features were zero backward payload (Bwd Packet Length Mean 0), a long Bwd IAT Max of about 92.8 s, and 45 forward PSH flags.

Re-scoring the 16 flows between the same pair put all of them above the alert threshold. Not all were labelled botnet: for example, 3067846 and 3070866 came back as botnet, 3066835 as brute_force, and 3068956 and 3069927 as dos.

A long-lived, persistent session on a non-standard port to a known attacker host, carrying mostly outbound pushed data, matches a bot reporting to its C2 server. That a second internal host contacted the same endpoint fits more than one infected machine sharing the same C2. The mixed family labels look like a weakness in the model's family classification, not a reason to doubt that the traffic is malicious.

recommended_actions.action: Isolate win-vista (192.168.10.8) and examine it for botnet malware, including persistence mechanisms and processes holding source port 1260.
Block outbound traffic to 205.174.165.73, especially TCP port 444, at the perimeter firewall.
Investigate 192.168.10.25 as a possible second bot, since it made repeated connections to the same C2 port.
Review the large volume of other traffic from 192.168.10.8 (SMB/NetBIOS on ports 135/139/445, DNS) for possible lateral movement or scanning.

uncertainties: Payloads are not visible, so it cannot be confirmed that commands were actually exchanged. The server sent back very little data (282 bytes over 16 flows), so whether the C2 achieved anything is unknown, and success_indicator is left false.
Some of the search results and prediction output came back truncated, so not every neighbouring flow was reviewed.
The detector named different attack families for different flows between the same pair (botnet, brute_force, dos).
I did not check whether any specific botnet malware, such as Ares, is associated with port 444, and I did not look up any CVE.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive. Workstation win-vista (192.168.10.8, Windows Vista, victim LAN) made repeated outbound TCP connections to 205.174.165.73, a known external Kali Linux attacker machine, on the non-standard port 444. Within ±30 minutes the tool found 15 flows between the pair besides this alert's flow (the tool leaves the alert's own flow out of its counts). They ran from 18:07 to 18:44. The connections were long (about 100 s for this flow) and carried only forward PSH-flagged traffic, with 0 backward payload bytes recorded. The detector flagged all 15 neighbouring flows, but its family label changes between dos and botnet. A victim host repeatedly calling out to an attacker machine on an unusual port looks like command-and-control (C2) callback or infiltration, not denial of service (DoS). So the predicted dos family is probably wrong. In the same window the host also sent 10,425 flows to 474 IPs on 1,071 ports, which fits internal reconnaissance from a compromised host.

findings.statement: 205.174.165.73 is a public address in zone attacker_external and is listed as a known attacker (Kali Linux attacker machine, external).
192.168.10.8 is win-vista: a Windows Vista 64-bit workstation in victim_lan, criticality medium, with no listed services.

The anchor flow went from 192.168.10.8:1260 to 205.174.165.73:444/TCP. It lasted about 99.9 s with 26 forward packets (6,658 bytes), 26 backward packets carrying 0 bytes, and no SYN, FIN or RST flags.

Within ±30 min of the anchor, the pair 192.168.10.8 → 205.174.165.73 had 15 flows besides the anchor, all to port 444. They were first seen at 18:07:13 and last seen at 18:44:24, and together carried 107,612 forward bytes and 0 backward bytes.
Within ±30 min, 192.168.10.8 also sent 10,425 flows to 474 distinct IPs on 1,071 distinct ports. Top ports were 53, 443, 80, 135, 139 and 445.
The detector scored the anchor flow at attack probability 0.98 with family dos (0.92). The biggest drivers were zero backward packet length, a large Bwd IAT Max and many Fwd PSH flags.
All 15 neighbouring flows between the pair scored above the alert threshold. Their family labels were split: several came out as botnet (about 0.99) and others as dos (about 0.97–0.99).

Repeated long-lived outbound sessions from a victim workstation to a known attacker host on a non-standard port look like a C2 or reverse-shell callback (T1571, possibly T1071), not a DoS attack. The broad scanning from the same host suggests it was compromised and then used for internal discovery.

recommended_actions.action: Isolate win-vista (192.168.10.8) from the network and collect a forensic image or memory dump to find the implant that is connecting to port 444.
Block 205.174.165.73 at the perimeter, especially TCP 444, and search other hosts for connections to it.
Review the hosts 192.168.10.8 reached during its sweep of 474 IPs and 1,071 ports (SMB on 445/139 and RPC on 135 in particular) for signs it moved further into the network.
Correct the alert's family from dos to C2 or infiltration, and report the inconsistent dos/botnet labelling for detector tuning.

uncertainties: The flows show 0 backward payload bytes even though there are 26 backward packets. Payload content and whether commands were actually exchanged cannot be checked from flow records, so success_indicator is left false, although an outbound callback suggests code already ran on the host.
The model's family label is unreliable for this pair (split between dos and botnet), and there is no infiltration or C2 class to choose from.
Whether any internal host other than 192.168.10.8 contacted 205.174.165.73 was not confirmed; the related-events summary lists no source hosts.
I did not test whether the 474-destination scan from this host is itself attack traffic.
I did not check how the host was first compromised or the period before 18:07.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive. Internal workstation win-vista (192.168.10.8, a Windows Vista machine in the victim LAN) kept sending data to 205.174.165.73 on TCP port 444. That address is a known external attacker machine (Kali Linux). Within ±30 minutes of the alert, the same source and destination had 13 long flows on port 444 between 18:12 and 18:44, all one way: 88,764 bytes went out and 0 payload bytes came back. Every one of the 13 neighbouring flows scored above the detector's alert threshold. The detector labels most of them botnet and some dos; I think the dos labels are wrong. No other internal host connected to this address. This looks like a single compromised workstation keeping a command-and-control (C2) or reverse-shell session open to the attacker over a non-standard port.

findings.statement: 205.174.165.73 is a public address in the attacker_external zone, flagged as a known attacker (Kali Linux attacker machine, external).

192.168.10.8 is win-vista, a Workstation running Windows Vista 64-bit in the victim_lan zone, with medium criticality and no listed services. Nothing in the record suggests it should talk to external hosts on port 444.

The alert flow lasted about 79.5 s, with 41 packets and 14,646 bytes going out and 39 packets with 0 payload bytes coming back. Within ±30 minutes, the same source-destination pair had 13 flows, all to port 444, between 18:12:30 and 18:44:24, totalling 88,764 bytes out and 0 bytes back.
All 13 flows to 205.174.165.73 in the window came from 192.168.10.8 (the same-destination and same-pair counts are identical). No other internal host contacted this address.
In the same window, 192.168.10.8 also sent 9,884 flows to 495 IPs across 1,051 ports, including ports 135, 139 and 445, plus 96 flows to port 1.

The detector gave the alert flow an attack probability of 0.994 and labelled it botnet (0.994). All 13 neighbouring flows for the pair also scored above the threshold. In the part of the output that was readable, some were labelled botnet and others dos, all with the same pattern: zero payload coming back and many PSH flags on outgoing packets.

Regular, long-lived, outbound-only sessions from a victim workstation to a known attacker host on non-standard port 444 fit C2 or reverse-shell activity. The dos labels on some flows are probably a family mix-up, since these are single low-volume sessions. The wide fan-out from the same host may be internal discovery after compromise, but I did not check that.
The host sent data out to the attacker repeatedly over about 30 minutes on established sessions. That suggests the compromise worked and the attacker has an active channel on win-vista.

recommended_actions.action: Isolate win-vista (192.168.10.8) from the network and collect a memory image and disk image to look for the implant or reverse-shell payload.
Block 205.174.165.73 at the perimeter on all ports, especially TCP 444, and search wider time ranges for any other host contacting it.

Review the host's internal fan-out in the same window (SMB/NetBIOS/RPC on ports 445, 139 and 135, and the broad port coverage) for signs of lateral movement or scanning, and check the internal hosts it reached.

uncertainties: No payloads were available, so I cannot say what protocol or C2 tool is running on port 444.
The detector output for the neighbouring flows was cut off, so I could not read the family label for every one of the 13 flows. All 13 were reported above the threshold.
I did not look up T1071 (Application Layer Protocol) or any CVEs, so I cannot say which exploit or delivery method led to the compromise.
Success is inferred from repeated established sessions sending data out to the attacker. I have no response content or host-level evidence to confirm it.
The fan-out of 9,884 flows from 192.168.10.8 was not analysed in detail. It may include normal traffic (DNS, HTTPS) as well as malicious activity.
the model asserted the attack succeeded, but no related-events aggregate shows a large return transfer to the source; severity was not raised for it

report.summary: This alert is a true positive web attack. Event 3196405 is a 34-second HTTP session from 172.16.0.1 to 192.168.10.50:80. 172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside (NAT) address and is marked as a known attacker: external attacker traffic shows up under this address. The target is web-server-16, a public web server rated high criticality, and its inventory notes list it as a target of the scheduled web attacks. Over ±30 minutes, 172.16.0.1 sent 1,550 flows to this server, all on port 80. The detector scored the anchor at 0.9994 as web_attack, driven by 101 forward PSH flags. 14 of the 15 neighbouring flows I scored stayed below the alert threshold, and their features show no payload. So the anchor is one of the few data-carrying sessions in a much larger HTTP burst, which fits web brute force or injection attempts. The evidence does not show that the attack succeeded.

findings.statement: Within ±30 min of the anchor, 172.16.0.1 sent 1,550 flows to one destination (192.168.10.50) on one port (80), between 12:28:38 and 13:28:36. Together they carried 3,119,428 forward bytes and 6,365,767 backward bytes.
The anchor flow lasted 34,020 ms, with 204 forward packets (43,906 bytes) and 105 backward packets (72,185 bytes), 2 SYN, 2 FIN and 0 RST.
In the same window, 192.168.10.50 also received traffic on port 22 (127 flows), port 21 (36 flows) and a set of single-flow high ports, across 39 distinct destination ports and 1,749 flows in total.

192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04 with HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22, rated high criticality in the victim_lan zone. Its notes list it as a target of the scheduled FTP/SSH brute force, DoS, web attacks and DDoS.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address and is flagged as a known attacker: external attacker traffic is NATed to this source address.

The detector gave the anchor an attack probability of 0.9994 (threshold 0.00024) and predicted web_attack with probability ~1.0. The top contributing features were Fwd PSH Flags = 101, Down/Up Ratio, Fwd Act Data Pkts = 101 and PSH Flag Count = 202.
Of 15 neighbouring flows on the same source–destination pair, only 1 scored above the threshold. The others scored about 1e-5 to 1.5e-4, and their features show zero-length payloads.

A long run of mostly empty or short HTTP connections, with a few long sessions that push many data packets, fits automated web attack tooling such as login brute force or injection against the public web application. That this server was scheduled as a web attack target supports the true-positive verdict.
The server returned 72 KB in the anchor session, but that alone does not show the attack worked: HTTP error or login pages could account for it.

recommended_actions.action: Review the web server's HTTP access logs (web-server-16) for 12:28–13:28 UTC. Find which URLs were requested and with what response codes, to tell brute force from XSS or SQL injection and to check whether any login succeeded.
Find the real external source behind the firewall's NAT (172.16.0.1) using the firewall's NAT/session logs, then block it at the perimeter.
Apply web application firewall rules and rate limits to HTTP/80 on 192.168.10.50, and audit the web application's accounts and database for signs of compromise.
Check the SSH/22 and FTP/21 traffic to the same host in this window as possible related brute-force activity.

uncertainties: No payloads or URLs were available, so I can't confirm the exact web attack subtype (brute force, XSS or SQL injection).
I didn't look up any CVEs because the inventory doesn't name the web application or its version.
Only 15 of the 1,550 flows on this pair were scored, and the predict_attack output was truncated, so I only have partial details for the neighbouring flows.
Because of the NAT through 172.16.0.1, the external attacker's real IP isn't visible in the flow data.
Nothing shows the attack succeeded, such as a successful login or data being exfiltrated.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive web attack on a high-criticality public web server. The source address, 172.16.0.1, is the firewall's inside NAT address, so these flows are external attacker traffic coming in through the firewall. Between 13:15 and 14:08 it sent 698 flows to 192.168.10.50 port 80, about 13 per minute, all to that one port. That steady, repeated pattern points to an automated tool rather than normal browsing. The detector gives the alerted flow a 0.96 attack probability with a web_attack family probability of 0.9996. Of 10 neighbouring flows rescored, 7 also crossed the alert threshold, but their predicted families were not all web_attack. The flow data does not show whether the attack worked.

findings.statement: Within ±30 minutes of event 3237435, 172.16.0.1 sent 698 flows, all to 192.168.10.50:80 and to no other host or port. They ran from 13:15:35 to 14:08:33 and totalled 888,204 bytes sent and 3,362,860 bytes returned. The alerted flow itself lasted about 5 seconds, with 5 packets and 599 bytes sent, and 5 packets and 2,021 bytes returned.
In the same window, 192.168.10.50 received 900 flows across 38 destination ports, mainly 80 (698), 22 (132) and 21 (35).

192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04 with HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22. It sits in the victim_lan zone with high criticality. The inventory notes say it is a scheduled target of web attacks, DoS, DDoS and FTP/SSH brute force.

172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address and is flagged as a known attacker. Traffic from external attackers appears under this address through NAT, so its flows into the victim LAN are attacker traffic.

The detector scored event 3237435 at an attack probability of 0.9576, against a threshold of 0.00024, and predicted web_attack with probability 0.9996. The features that pushed the score up most were Bwd Init Win Bytes = 236 and Packet Length Max = 2021.

Of 11 flows from the same source and destination pair that were rescored, 8 were above the threshold, including the anchor. Event 3315980 was predicted as web_attack. Event 3149822 was predicted as brute_force. Events 3133104, 3270260 and 3289406 were below the threshold.

Close to 700 HTTP sessions from one NAT'd attacker address to one web server in under an hour looks like automated web attack tooling, such as brute force, XSS or SQL injection, rather than a person browsing. This fits the server being a scheduled web attack target.

recommended_actions.action: Review web-server-16's HTTP access and application logs from 13:15 to 14:08 on 2017-07-06. Look for requests carrying injection or XSS payloads, repeated login attempts, and any successful (2xx) responses to suspicious requests.
Use the firewall's NAT translation logs to find the real external source behind 172.16.0.1, then block it or rate-limit it at the perimeter.
Put a WAF in front of the public web server or tighten its rules. Also check the SSH (22) and FTP (21) traffic to the same host in this window for related brute-force activity.

uncertainties: The flow records contain no payloads, so the specific web attack (brute force, XSS or SQL injection) cannot be confirmed, and neither can its success.
Part of the predict_attack output was truncated, so the scores of the last few neighbouring flows could not be checked.
No web server software or version is recorded for 192.168.10.50, so no CVE lookup was done.
Some neighbouring flows were classed as brute_force or fell below the threshold, so the pair's traffic is not all labelled web_attack.

report.summary: This alert is very likely a real web attack. The detector scored event 3254826 at 0.9994 and labelled it web_attack. The flow came from 172.16.0.1, the firewall's NAT address that external attackers' traffic appears behind. It went to web-server-16 (192.168.10.50:80), a high-criticality public web server, and was part of 1549 HTTP flows between the same two hosts within ±30 minutes. The flow lasted about 33 s and carried many requests (101 forward packets with the PSH flag set, i.e. 101 data-carrying pushes). That pattern fits automated web attack traffic such as a login brute force or XSS. Only 1 of 20 neighbouring flows I sampled crossed the alert threshold, and the ones visible in the output carried no payload. So the attack payload appears in a small share of the burst. There is no evidence that the attack succeeded.

findings.statement: Within ±30 minutes of the anchor, 172.16.0.1 sent 1549 flows, all to 192.168.10.50 on port 80 only, with 3,243,878 bytes forward and 6,361,442 bytes back. The anchor flow lasted 32.9 s, with 204 forward packets (43,951 bytes) and 105 backward packets (72,209 bytes). In the same window the destination also received 125 flows on port 22 and 37 on port 21.

192.168.10.50 is web-server-16: a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04 with HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22, criticality high, zone victim_lan. The asset notes list it as a scheduled target of web attacks.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address and is flagged as a known attacker. External attacker traffic reaches the victim LAN through NAT using this address.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive. Event 3289046 is a 33-second HTTP session from 172.16.0.1 to port 80 on web-server-16 (192.168.10.50), a public web server rated high criticality. The enrichment record names 172.16.0.1 as the firewall's inside NAT address, so traffic from it is external attacker traffic coming through the firewall. In this one session the client sent 204 packets, 101 of them carrying data with the PSH flag set, and the server answered with 72 KB. That looks like many scripted HTTP requests on one connection, which fits automated web attack tooling such as login brute force. The detector scored the flow at about 0.9993 with family web_attack. The same source opened 1,551 port-80 flows to this server within ±30 minutes, which suggests automation. However, the 10 sampled neighbouring flows scored far below the alert threshold, and their features suggest they carried no data. So only this flow is confirmed as the attack session, and nothing shows that the attack succeeded.

findings.statement: The anchor flow 3289046 (172.16.0.1:51042 -> 192.168.10.50:80/TCP) lasted 33,006 ms. The client sent 204 packets (43,951 bytes) and the server returned 105 packets (72,209 bytes), with 2 SYN, 2 FIN and 0 RST.

Within ±30 minutes, 172.16.0.1 sent 1,551 flows, all to 192.168.10.50 on port 80, between 12:29:10 and 13:29:08 UTC. Together they carried 3,123,613 bytes forward and 6,476,763 bytes back. The detector scored the anchor flow at about 0.9993 against a threshold of about 0.00024 and gave web_attack a family probability of about 1.0. The features that pushed the score up most were Fwd PSH Flags=101, Down/Up Ratio≈0.51, Fwd Act Data Pkts=101 and PSH Flag Count=202.

The anchor looks like one keep-alive HTTP session with about 101 separate client data pushes in 33 seconds, which matches scripted repeated requests such as a form-login brute force or injection attempts. The large number of other port-80 flows from the same NAT'd attacker address supports an automated campaign. The neighbours that look empty were not detected as attacks.

There are no payloads, so we can't tell whether any request succeeded. The 72 KB in replies is consistent with the server returning a page over and over and does not by itself show a successful login or exploit.

recommended_actions.action: Review the HTTP access and application logs on web-server-16 for around 12:59 UTC, especially POSTs to login pages and request parameters containing script or SQL patterns, to identify the sub-technique and check whether any login succeeded.
Use the firewall's NAT translation logs to map 172.16.0.1 back to the real external source address(es), then block or rate-limit them.
Put WAF or rate-limiting rules in front of the HTTP service on this high-criticality public server.
Look into the SSH and FTP flows to the same server in the same window as a possible related brute-force activity.

uncertainties: Without payloads, we can't tell whether this was brute force, XSS or SQL injection; the family label comes only from the model.
Only 10 of the 1,551 flows on this source/destination pair were scored, and all came out benign-looking. How many other flows in the campaign are real attack sessions is unknown.
The web application running on the server is not identified, so no CVE lookup was done and no CVE is attributed.
No evidence shows whether the attack succeeded (for example a session cookie being issued or a login succeeding).

report.summary: The detector rated event 3300170 at probability 0.276, which is far above its very low threshold of 0.00024, and labelled it dos at 0.82 (port_scan 0.18). It goes from 172.16.0.1, the firewall's NAT address that hides external sources, to FTP port 21 on web-server-16, a high-criticality host. The anchor has no SYN, but two FIN flags. It reuses source port 50833 from event 3096118 about two minutes earlier, so it looks like the closing tail of an existing FTP session. Over ±30 minutes this source sent only 29 flows, to 2 hosts and 3 ports (mostly 80 and 21). There were 8 small FTP sessions over about 25 minutes, each under 60 bytes. That does not fit DoS flooding, a port scan, or a high-rate brute-force burst. Neighbouring flows got mixed scores: 15 of 21 crossed the threshold, but with probabilities near 1e-3, and with both dos and port_scan labels. Because 172.16.0.1 carries all NAT'd external traffic, harmless and malicious traffic cannot be told apart by source address alone. The evidence does not support a confident true or false positive, so an analyst should decide.

findings.statement: Anchor flow 3300170: TCP from 172.16.0.1:50833 to 192.168.10.50:21. 3 packets / 6 bytes forward, 4 packets / 14 bytes back, 1.709 ms, 0 SYN, 2 FIN.

uncertainties: Because of NAT, the real external source behind 172.16.0.1 cannot be identified, so attacker and harmless traffic through the firewall cannot be separated.
No payloads or FTP application logs were available, so login attempts or their outcome could not be checked.
